strengths: The paper provides a broad, multi-faceted empirical study of Mamba-based HuBERT models, spanning computational efficiency, long-context ASR, streaming/causal ASR, phone purity of quantized units, CCA-based representation analysis, and SUPERB probing — a more comprehensive treatment than prior single-task Mamba speech studies.

The long-context ASR and streaming ASR experiments make a clear, practically relevant point: Mamba's linear scaling avoids the OOM failures of Transformer-based HuBERT on long inputs, and yields lower WER when full-document context is available.

The representation analysis (phone purity across k-means granularities, CCA with phoneme/speaker/emotion embeddings) is a reasonable set of tools to probe qualitative differences between architectures, and the paper reports some non-trivial dissociations (e.g., phone purity not predicting fine-tuning performance).
The inclusion of an ablation between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba, and a naive 'Transformer + Causal Mask' baseline, adds useful nuance rather than only reporting favorable comparisons for Mamba.
weaknesses: Pretraining deviates substantially from standard HuBERT recipes (single GPU, 8x larger per-GPU batch resulting in ~1/4 the audio seen per batch versus the original setup), which raises concerns about whether the base Transformer baseline is well-trained and whether comparisons reflect genuine architectural differences or under-trained baselines; this also limits reproducibility relative to widely-used checkpoints.

Statistical rigor is inconsistent: a paired t-test is reported for only one comparison (long-context vs utterance-level WER), while all other central comparisons (SUPERB probing tables, phone purity, CCA) rely on single runs with no variance estimates or repeated seeds, making it hard to judge whether reported gaps (e.g., 823.15 vs 805.44 SUPERBS, or small PR differences) are meaningful or noise.

Results are mixed and sometimes contradict the paper's overall framing: bidirectional base-size ExtBiMamba clearly underperforms Transformer across all four SUPERB tasks, and the choice between ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba flips with model scale, undermining the generality of claims that Mamba is a 'promising and complementary direction' — the paper acknowledges this but the abstract/conclusion still leans optimistic.

Experimental scale is limited to base/small model sizes and a small number of datasets (TEDLIUM3 for long-context ASR; an unspecified/underspecified dataset for causal ASR), so claims about scalability and generalizability of the findings are not well supported beyond the tested regime.

Reproducibility details are sparse: hyperparameters for fine-tuning experiments, exact SUPERB downstream configurations, and pretraining corpus/preprocessing are not clearly specified in the excerpt, and no code/checkpoint release is mentioned.

The contribution is primarily an empirical benchmarking/exploration study without a new architectural or methodological innovation; the observations (linear-time scaling advantages, causal Mamba benefits) are largely expected from Mamba's known properties and prior single-task studies cited in the related work, limiting the paper's novelty.

The paper's focus, framing, and formatting (IEEE speech-conference style, ASR/SUPERB benchmarks) sit at the periphery of core ACL/NLP topics, and the paper does not connect its findings to broader NLP implications (e.g., long-context language modeling, spoken dialogue systems) beyond a brief mention of spoken language models as consumers of the SSL units.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely comprehensive, multi-faceted evaluation of Mamba-based HuBERT models spanning fine-tuning (utterance-level, document-level long-context, streaming/causal ASR), representation analysis (phone purity via k-means, CCA with phonetic/speaker/emotion attributes), and downstream probing (SUPERB subset) in both causal and bidirectional settings -- addressing a real gap noted in related work, where prior Mamba-for-speech studies were limited to isolated tasks.

The efficiency argument (near-constant MACs/RTF vs. sequence length, avoidance of OOM beyond 80s for Causal Transformer) is well-motivated and empirically demonstrated, and translates into a concrete, practically meaningful result: document-level fine-tuning that Transformer cannot even run improves WER from 13.37% to 11.08%.

The causal-setting results (Mamba fine-tuned ASR and SUPERB probing) are consistently favorable and internally consistent with the phone-purity/CCA analyses, giving a coherent story for at least one clear regime (causal/streaming) where Mamba is advantageous.

The paper is scientifically honest about negative/mixed findings (e.g., ExtBiMamba underperforming Transformer at base size in bidirectional probing, phone purity not correlating with ASR fine-tuning performance) rather than only reporting favorable numbers, and it offers a thoughtful ablation (ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba) exploring architectural variants.
Relevant citation and contextualization within existing Mamba-for-speech and SSL literature, clarifying the paper's distinct contribution relative to closest prior work (e.g., Zhang et al.).
weaknesses: Pretraining is conducted under a substantially non-standard, compute-constrained regime (single GPU, larger per-GPU batch but only ~1/4 the total audio duration per batch versus original HuBERT), and no comparison is made against publicly available, standard-trained HuBERT checkpoints; this limits how much the comparative claims ('Mamba outperforms Transformer counterpart') generalize beyond this specific constrained setup, since both architectures may be affected differently by under-training.

Virtually all quantitative comparisons (Tables I-V) appear to be single-run point estimates without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, except for one paired t-test on the long-context result; several conclusions rest on small numeric gaps (e.g., SUPERBS 766.94 vs. 767.70, or PR 11.68 vs 11.72) that are not shown to be statistically meaningful, weakening the rigor of claims drawn from Tables III-V.

The core motivating narrative (Mamba as a strong alternative to Transformer for speech SSL) is substantially undermined by the bidirectional base-size results, where ExtBiMamba underperforms Transformer across nearly all SUPERB metrics; the paper's summary bullet points still claim general superiority for 'causal architecture,' but the broader bidirectional story is scale-dependent and inconsistent (ExtBiMamba wins small, loses base; InnBiMamba wins base, loses small), and this inconsistency is not mechanistically explained, only post-hoc rationalized.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact pretraining corpus/hours, hyperparameters, number of training runs, and code/checkpoint release are not clearly specified, which is important given the atypical training regime used.

The SUPERB evaluation is restricted to 4 of the full benchmark's tasks (via MiniSUPERB rationale), somewhat limiting the scope of generalization claims about representation quality across the full range of speech understanding tasks.

The work is primarily a speech-processing systems/engineering study; its direct relevance to core NLP/computational-linguistics research questions is comparatively narrow, situating it more naturally as a solid empirical contribution than a broadly impactful NLP finding.

strengths: Comprehensive, multi-faceted empirical investigation of Mamba-based HuBERT models covering fine-tuning (long-context ASR, streaming/causal ASR), representation analysis (phone purity, CCA with phonetic/speaker/emotion attributes), and downstream probing (SUPERB) in both causal and bidirectional settings—addressing the stated gap that prior work only evaluates Mamba on isolated tasks.

Clear and practically relevant efficiency results (MACs/RTF vs. sequence length) that convincingly demonstrate Mamba's linear-time advantage and the Transformer's OOM failure on long sequences, directly supporting the long-context ASR use case.

Useful ablation between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba variants, with an attempt to explain the observed scale-dependent behavior via training-loss-scale/instability analysis (Appendix D), adding some mechanistic insight beyond pure benchmark numbers.

Transparent and honest limitations section acknowledging reduced-scale/single-GPU training and its effect on absolute performance relative to official HuBERT baselines, which aids interpretability of the reported trends.

Additional appendices (full SUPERB evaluation on 10 tasks, extra k-means cluster settings) that check robustness of the four-task subset conclusions, strengthening the credibility of the probing claims.
weaknesses: Nearly all reported results are from a single training/fine-tuning run without seeds or repeated trials (explicitly stated), so many of the comparative claims (e.g., 15.77% vs 16.66% WER, or small SUPERBS score differences) lack any measure of variance; only one paired t-test is reported for a single comparison, which is insufficient to support the many other performance-gap claims made throughout the paper.

Pretraining is conducted with a batch size ~1/4 of the original HuBERT setup on a single V100 GPU, and the paper itself notes their Transformer-based HuBERT underperforms the official FAIR-released model. This raises concerns about whether conclusions (especially about bidirectional Mamba's 'limited scalability') are artifacts of under-trained/resource-constrained models rather than intrinsic architectural properties, since the compared Transformer baselines are also weaker than standard, but the degree of degradation may differ between architectures.

The central narrative is largely a collection of empirical observations (causal Mamba is good, bidirectional Mamba scales poorly) without a deeper mechanistic explanation beyond post-hoc hypotheses about training instability (which are themselves only weakly substantiated via a qualitative loss-scale plot rather than controlled experiments, e.g., gradient clipping variations or multiple seeds).

Novelty relative to closely related prior work (e.g., Zhang et al. 2025's Mamba-based SSL analysis) is asserted but not deeply contrasted; the paper's claim of being the 'first comprehensive exploration' could be more rigorously justified against this and other concurrent works.

Some architectural/complexity confounds are not fully controlled: comparisons mix models of different parameter counts (e.g., 78.2M Mamba vs 94.7M Transformer) when claiming superiority, which somewhat complicates clean attribution of gains to the architecture itself versus other design choices (e.g., presence/absence of MLP).

strengths: Fills a clear gap in the literature: prior Mamba-for-speech-SSL work examined isolated tasks, whereas this paper provides a genuinely comprehensive, cross-task study (long-context ASR, streaming/causal ASR, SUPERB probing across four and then ten tasks, phone purity, CCA-based representational analysis) under a unified experimental framework.

The experiments are methodologically sound and fairly rigorous for an exploratory/empirical paper: consistent training pipelines for both Mamba and Transformer baselines, matched parameter counts where possible, ablations across model sizes (Base/Small) and bidirectional variants (ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba), a statistical significance test (paired t-test) for the long-context ASR result, and a dedicated appendix validating that SUPERB-subset trends hold on the full 10-task benchmark.

The paper reports honest, non-cherry-picked findings, including negative/mixed results (e.g., ExtBiMamba underperforming Transformer at Base scale, scalability challenges in the bidirectional setting), which strengthens credibility and gives the community actionable design guidance rather than an over-claimed 'Mamba wins everywhere' narrative.

Multiple analysis angles (phone purity, CCA with phoneme/speaker/emotion attributes, training-loss-scale stability plots) converge to give a coherent mechanistic story about why/where Mamba-based SSL models help, going beyond simple leaderboard numbers.

Efficiency claims (MACs, RTF, OOM behavior) are empirically substantiated with concrete measurements across a wide range of sequence lengths (5s–320s/5min), directly supporting the paper's central motivating claim about linear-time scaling.
Code availability and detailed description of hyperparameters/training pipeline support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Due to single-GPU compute constraints, the batch size is roughly 1/4 of the original HuBERT setup, and the authors' own Transformer-based HuBERT trained under this regime underperforms the official FAIR-released model; this raises the concern that some Transformer vs. Mamba comparisons may be skewed by an under-trained Transformer baseline rather than reflecting a fundamental architectural advantage.

Most pretraining and fine-tuning results appear to come from single training runs without multiple seeds (the only reported significance test is a paired t-test on WER, not on training variance), leaving open questions about the robustness/reproducibility of some numerically close comparisons (e.g., small-size probing scores that differ by only a few points).

Findings about limited bidirectional scalability are based only on Base and Small scale models; without evidence at larger scales, the claim that Mamba 'suffers from limited scalability' remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated trend, and the explanation (training instability inferred from loss-scale oscillation plots) is somewhat speculative.

Parameter counts are not always matched across compared models (e.g., 78.2M Mamba vs. 94.7M Causal Transformer), which the paper flags positively as an efficiency advantage but which also complicates strictly controlled comparison of architectural effects.

The core methodological contribution is primarily an empirical/exploratory swap of Transformer blocks for existing Mamba variants (ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba from prior work) combined with established evaluation protocols (SUPERB, phone purity, CCA); there is limited technical novelty in modeling or methodology beyond the systematic evaluation itself.

Some conclusions are mixed and not fully resolved within the paper (e.g., InnBiMamba better at Base but worse at Small, and the disconnect between phone purity trends and PR probing results is only partially explained), leaving the practical takeaway on which bidirectional variant to use somewhat unclear for practitioners.
